report.source_text: Laboratory tests were remarkable for acute on chronic kidney injury (serum creatinine 3.63 mg/dL, baseline 2.93 mg/dL) (normal range 0.6–1.2 mg/dL) and hyperglycaemia 597 mg/dL (normal range 70–99 mg/dL). Thyroid stimulating hormone was 2.6 (normal range 0.4–4.2 mcU/mL). Venous blood gas showed pH 7.34, serum bicarbonate was 21 mmol/L (normal range 22–29). Urinalysis showed no ketosis. Calculated serum osmolarity was 308 mosm/kg (normal 280–305 mosm/kg) making hyperosmolar hyperglycaemia state unlikely. Hb A1c level returned elevated at 17.0% (normal <6.0%).

report.source_text: The patient was admitted to the hospital for further management. Intravenous hydration and subcutaneous basal and prandial insulin were administered. Serum blood glucose levels normalised over the next 24–48 hours. Severe hemichorea-hemiballismus persisted, which impaired his ambulation and sleep. Due to severe insomnia and overnight agitation, the patient was initially treated with escalating doses of olanzapine. Low-dose clonazepam was added to the regimen on day 3 hospitalisation with minimal improvement. On day 4 olanzapine was stopped and risperidone 2 mg nightly was started with improvement in both sleep and right arm and right leg chorea-hemiballismus. The patient’s clinical symptoms of hemichorea-hemiballismus were markedly improved prior to discharge on hospital day 6.

report.source_text: He was discharged to an acute rehabilitation facility with subcutaneous insulin, sitagliptin and risperidone with plans for ambulatory follow-up with endocrinology and neurology. The patient completed a successful course of acute rehabilitation following hospital discharge. Two months post-hospitalisation the intensity and frequency of the patient’s hemichorea involving the right upper and lower extremity had decreased and he had returned to all his usual activities. At 6-month follow-up, mild chorea in his right arm persisted.

clinician.trajectory_summary: An elderly man (mid-80s) with uncontrolled type 2 diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 17.0%), chronic kidney disease stage 4, and multiple comorbidities presented to the emergency department with acute onset (1-day history) of right-sided hemichorea and hemiballismus with hyperkinetic dyskinesia preventing voluntary movement. At admission, he had severe hyperglycemia (597 mg/dL), acute on chronic kidney injury (creatinine 3.63 mg/dL), mild metabolic acidosis (pH 7.34, bicarbonate 21 mmol/L), and elevated serum osmolarity (308 mosm/kg), but no ketosis. Brain imaging (CT and MRI) revealed hyperdensity and increased T1 signal intensity in the left basal ganglia (lentiform nucleus, caudate nucleus, and putamen) with critical sparing of the internal capsule, excluding acute ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke. The patient was admitted and treated with intravenous hydration and subcutaneous insulin, with blood glucose normalizing over 24-48 hours. Despite glycemic control, severe hemichorea-hemiballismus persisted initially, requiring antipsychotic therapy. Olanzapine was escalated with minimal benefit; risperidone 2 mg nightly was initiated on hospital day 4 with marked improvement in both sleep and chorea-hemiballismus. The patient was discharged on hospital day 6 with markedly improved symptoms and completed acute rehabilitation. At 2-month follow-up, hemichorea intensity and frequency had substantially decreased with return to usual activities. At 6-month follow-up, only mild residual chorea in the right arm persisted.
